column4: The section's named waḍaʿa root and wording “from them” describe taking a burden off its bearer; here the Prophet “يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ” people's burdens and fetters. This extends the same relief to a community, though these restraints need not be the same guilt-load.

The section's dictionary gloss for vizr includes goods packed and carried; after the calf episode, the people say they were loaded with “أَوْزَارًا مِّن زِينَةِ الْقَوْمِ.” Here awzār means actual ornaments, preserving the concrete sense before the section's move to sin as a load.

The section's named lexeme vizr links sin with physical weight and names zahr as the back; when the Hour catches the deniers, “يَحْمِلُونَ أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ.” Their sins remain on their backs, reversing the removed load.

The section's named vizr as a sin-load is left behind by its addressee; here the one who turns away from the Reminder “يَحْمِلُ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ وِزْرًا.” This is the inverse: turning from remembrance leaves a burden to carry.

Following 20:100's burden for turning away from the Reminder, this ayah calls the coming weight “حِمْلًا” and says it is a bad load for them. Its own contribution is to make the burden's outcome explicit, opposite the load's removal.

The section's named vizr connects sin to weight; this judgment rule says “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَىٰ,” and even a heavily loaded soul gets no part of its burden carried. It sets the limit that one person's guilt is not removed by another human, unlike God's removal in the section.

The section's vizr is a sin-load taken off its bearer; here those who mislead will bear their own full burdens and additional burdens from those they misled. The image reverses relief into an added consequence for leading others astray.

This ayah answers the offer in 29:12: the deceivers will indeed bear their own burdens and further burdens alongside them. It clarifies that misleaders add liability through their own act; they do not simply substitute for those they misled.

This ayah's contribution is the unbelievers' false offer to carry the believers' errors if they follow their way; 29:13 answers it. The section's named burden-transfer image thus meets an explicit, rejected promise to take another's load.

The section's named lexeme vizr is also used in this rule the Prophet is told to state: no bearer carries another's burden. In its own context it grounds each soul's accountability, bounding the section's removal as God's act rather than a person's substitution.

The section's vizr is a burden removed from its bearer; this ayah says no bearer bears another's burden, then ties guidance to each soul and says punishment waits for a messenger. The personal-responsibility rule marks the opposite boundary.

This ayah repeats the section's named vizr formula that no bearer carries another's burden, while saying God has no need of disbelief and is pleased with gratitude. Its context underscores personal answerability rather than a transferable load.

The section's named vizr formula appears in the account of what was made known to Moses and Abraham: no bearer bears another's burden. This places the removal image beside a repeated rule of individual liability.

The section's load is taken off its carrier; here believers pray, “رَبَّنَا وَلَا تَحْمِلْ عَلَيْنَا إِصْرًا,” asking that a heavy burden not be laid on them. It turns the removal image into a communal plea against imposed weight.

The section leaves the removed burden unnamed; the same divine “We” tells the Prophet, “قَوْلًا ثَقِيلًا” will be cast upon him. A heavy revelation commission can coexist with relief from another burden.

The section portrays a load removed from the Prophet; this ayah sets a boundary on the mission's hardship, saying the Quran was not sent to make him suffer. Its own contribution is the stated purpose of the revelation, not another named load.

The section does not identify the burden on the Prophet's back; this ayah names a distinct trust that the heavens, earth, and mountains declined and the human being carried, “وَحَمَلَهَا الْإِنسَانُ.” It gives a separate image of weighty responsibility rather than identifying the removed load.

Immediately after 53:38 says one bearer does not carry another's burden, this ayah says a person has only what they strive for. Its own contribution is to connect the load rule with responsibility for one's effort.

The section's wording “from you” presents weight taken off its bearer; this ayah says God wants to lighten things for people because the human being was created weak. It states the same concern for human capacity without naming the particular burden.

The section develops the literal sense of a load borne on a back; this ayah says livestock carry people's loads to distant lands they could not reach without hardship. It places bodily weight within travel and the mercy of being carried.

The section's dictionary picture is a bundle of possessions carried as a load; in the cup-search, the reward offered is “حِمْلُ بَعِيرٍ,” a camel's load. This is a concrete cargo measure, though its context is a promised reward rather than a burden removed.

The section's load is bodily weight; this ayah compares those entrusted with Torah who do not carry it out to a donkey carrying books, “يَحْمِلُ أَسْفَارًا.” The physical load remains while its intended responsibility is unmet.

The section opens with the body's front, the chest, alongside the burdened back; Moses asks, “رَبِّ اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي.” The next ayah, 20:26, completes his request by asking ease for his task, joining chest-opening to capacity for a mission.

This continuation asks God to make Moses' task easy, following his request for an expanded chest in 20:25. Its own contribution links relief in the work to the preceding bodily image of an opened chest.

The section's first bodily image is an opened chest; here God expands the chest of the one He guides toward Islam and makes the disbeliever's chest tight. The same bodily site carries receptivity or constriction, clarifying the spiritual context of opening.

This ayah describes a person whose chest God has expanded for Islam and who is then upon light from his Lord. It parallels the section's opened chest as a change in inward capacity, while naming guidance as its context.

The section presents an opened chest at the front of the body; Moses says his chest tightens and his tongue is not fluent as he faces Pharaoh. This is a specific reversal of the opened-chest image under the strain of a prophetic task.

The Prophet's chest is described as tight because of what people say; this reverses the section's opened chest. The next ayah, 15:98, directs him to glorify his Lord and prostrate, completing the passage's response to that distress.

The section's image opens the Prophet's chest as relief; this ayah describes someone who opens his breast to disbelief, a contrary use of the same bodily image. It marks that an opened chest's meaning depends on what it receives.

The section's raised remembrance is paired here with houses God permits “أَن تُرْفَعَ” and where “اسْمُهُ” is remembered. The raised place and remembered name meet in one scene, though the ayah concerns houses of worship rather than the Prophet's mention.

The section's named rafaʿ wording raises remembrance; here good speech ascends to God and righteous deeds are said to raise it, “وَالْعَمَلُ الصَّالِحُ يَرْفَعُهُ.” This gives spoken good and its elevation a parallel, with God as the destination.
The section says the Prophet's remembrance is raised; this ayah says God raised Idris to a high station. Its own image is the elevation of a prophet's standing, not his name.

The section's named rafaʿ image makes remembrance rise; this ayah says God raises believers and those given knowledge in degrees. It offers a specific parallel of elevated standing while naming faith and knowledge as its measure.

The section's raised object is the Prophet's remembrance; this ayah speaks of God raising some people above others in degrees as livelihood is apportioned. It contrasts elevated mention with worldly rank and provision.

The section's dictionary note for rafaʿ includes physically lifting with a cord and hand; this ayah depicts Abraham and Ishmael raising the foundations of the House. It gives the root's concrete lifting action a building scene, while 94:4 applies it to remembrance.

The section's dictionary account locates the back's creaking in joints and ribs; this creation ayah names the backbone and ribs as paired bodily landmarks. It concerns fluid and human creation, not weight or sound, so the link is anatomical only.

The section's image places weight on a person's back; this ayah says people sit on the backs of cattle and ships, then recalls God's favor in carrying them. Its own contribution reverses the bearer: an animal's back supports the person rather than the person's back bearing a load.

The section's dictionary picture begins with possessions carried as a load and turns vizr toward sin; here hoarded gold and silver are heated and used to brand foreheads, sides, and backs. It does not say they carry the wealth, so the specific link is wealth turning into a bodily mark, not a carried burden.

The section's named waḍaʿa root means lowering or putting down a load; at the terror of the Hour this ayah says every pregnant woman will put down what she carries. It is a literal bodily load released by terror, opposite the section's relief.

The section's image makes weight borne by a body audible on the back; this ayah says a mother carried her child with hardship and delivered him with hardship. Its own contribution is a distinct bodily burden at pregnancy and birth, not a guilt-load or a back-load.

The section's dictionary gloss for vizr begins with a physical load; in this ayah a spouse carries a light pregnancy that later becomes heavy. The load is internal rather than on the back, so this is a limited parallel in how bodily weight grows.

The section's dictionary detail pictures a prisoner's cord lifting a fetter; this ayah puts chains around the necks of people who deny resurrection. Its own contribution is restraint retained as judgment, opposite the section's removal of burden.

The section connects misleaders with extra burdens carried at judgment; in this ayah the misled and their arrogant leaders dispute blame, then shackles are placed on the disbelievers' necks. It joins misguidance with a distinct restraint scene rather than transferring the load.

The section's dictionary note describes a bound person lifting a fetter's cord; this ayah places collars on necks up to the chins, leaving the people with their heads held up. Its own image is a posture forced by fetters, opposite a restraint being lifted by its bearer.

The section's dictionary detail links a prisoner's raised fetter-cord to restraint; this ayah pictures collars on necks and chains as people are dragged. Its own contribution is a body still bound at judgment, reversing the release image.

The section's dictionary note evokes the prisoner's hand lifting the cord of a fetter; this ayah commands that a condemned man be seized and shackled. Its own contribution is the act of binding, the contrary state to a load or restraint taken off.

The section's dictionary detail evokes a cord attached to a fetter; this ayah specifies a chain seventy cubits long into which the condemned man is thrust. The preceding punishment passage orders him shackled at 69:30; this ayah contributes the chain's length and continued restraint.

The section develops a prisoner's fetter and the rope by which it is raised; this ayah names shackles and fire among the punishments prepared for its deniers. It supplies the retained-restraint side of the contrast.

The section's dictionary note describes a bound person's fetter; this ayah says chains and shackles have been prepared for the disbelievers. Its own contribution is explicit punishment by restraints, the inverse of restraints being removed.

The section's dictionary detail involves a prisoner and his fetter; this ayah depicts criminals thrown into a narrow place while bound together. The restraint remains in place, the contrary state to the section's load being taken off.
